title: Wiener v. United States (1958)
shortTitle: Wiener v. United States (1958) — assigned excerpt
summary: The President may not remove at will a member of an adjudicatory commission whose statute is silent on removal, because the nature of the adjudicating function implies independence from executive control.
notes:
Key line: For such is this case, we are compelled to conclude that no such power is given to the President directly by the Constitution, and none is impliedly conferred upon him by statute simply because Congress said nothing about it. (Justice Frankfurter)

Citation: 357 U.S. 349 (1958).

sections.Parties: The petitioner was Myron Wiener, a member of the War Claims Commission who had been nominated by President Truman, confirmed by the Senate on June 2, 1950, and sworn in on June 8, 1950. The respondent was the United States, sued in the Court of Claims for the salary Wiener would have earned between his removal by President Eisenhower in December 1953 and the Commission's abolition on June 30, 1954. I. H. Wachtel argued for Wiener; Solicitor General J. Lee Rankin argued for the Government. The Commission itself, a three-member body of which at least two members had to be lawyers, was the institutional focus of the dispute.
sections.Material Facts: The War Claims Act of 1948, 62 Stat. 1240, gave the Commission jurisdiction to receive and adjudicate according to law claims for compensating internees, prisoners of war and religious organizations injured by the enemy in the Second World War. Its decisions were to be final and not subject to review by any other official or any court. The Commission was to wind up within three years after the deadline for filing claims, a deadline Congress extended to March 31, 1952. The Act contained no provision for removing a Commissioner. On December 10, 1953, after Wiener refused a request to resign, President Eisenhower removed him, writing that he regarded it as in the national interest to complete administration of the Act with personnel of his own selection. Reorganization Plan No. 1 of 1954 abolished the Commission on July 1, 1954.
sections.Procedural History: Wiener sued in the Court of Claims for his salary from his removal to June 30, 1954, the last day of the Commission's existence. A divided Court of Claims dismissed the petition, 135 Ct. Cl. 827, 142 F. Supp. 910. The Supreme Court granted certiorari, 352 U.S. 980, because the case presented a variant of the constitutional problem decided in Myers v. United States and Humphrey's Executor v. United States. The Court heard argument on November 18, 1957, and decided the case on June 30, 1958, reversing the Court of Claims. Justice Frankfurter wrote for a unanimous Court.
sections.Issue: Did the President have power, either under Article II directly or by implication from a statute that said nothing about removal, to remove a member of the War Claims Commission before the end of the Commission's statutory life simply because he wanted his own appointees to administer the Act? The question required the Court to decide whether the rule of Myers v. United States, recognizing an illimitable presidential removal power over executive officers, or the rule of Humphrey's Executor, protecting members of quasi-judicial bodies, governed a body whose statute fixed no term and mentioned no grounds for removal.
sections.Holding: No. The President had no power under the Constitution or the Act to remove Wiener, and the Court of Claims erred in dismissing his suit. Humphrey's Executor narrowed Myers to purely executive officers and established that Congress may insulate officers who adjudicate from presidential control. The War Claims Commission was an adjudicating body whose decisions Congress made final and unreviewable, so Congress must have intended it to act free from executive influence. The absence of an express removal provision does not supply a removal power; where the function is judicial in character, the inference runs the other way. Judgment reversed.
sections.Reasoning: Justice Frankfurter framed the case within the history of the removal power. Myers had announced a broad presidential power to remove executive officers, but Humphrey's Executor, decided nine years later, confined Myers to its facts and held that the President could not remove a Federal Trade Commissioner at will because the Commission exercised quasi-legislative and quasi-judicial functions and Congress meant it to be independent. Humphrey's Executor drew a sharp line between executive officers who serve as the President's arm and officers whose duties require freedom from executive interference. The most reliable factor for inferring removal power, Frankfurter wrote, is the nature of the function Congress vested in the body. The War Claims Commission was created to adjudicate claims according to law, and Congress went further than in the Trade Commission Act by making its decisions final and unreviewable by any official or court. That design shows Congress wanted the Commission to decide on the merits of each claim, free from the influence of any other official. Congress's failure to provide for removal cannot be read as leaving the President free; if anything, the intrinsic judicial character of the task means Congress did not want the President to intervene. The President's stated reason, a wish for personnel of his own selection, was exactly the kind of control Humphrey's Executor forbade. No power to remove was given by the Constitution, and none was implied by statutory silence.

topics.lrs-s-agency-independence: Adjudicatory function supported an inference of protection even without express for-cause language.
topics.lrs-s-removal: A preference for different personnel did not justify this removal from an adjudicatory commission.
topics.lrs-s-ftc-tenure: Wiener extends the Humphrey's Executor reasoning about adjudicatory bodies to a statute silent on removal, so the FTC tenure provision is the natural comparison.

learning.separateOpinions: None. Justice Frankfurter wrote for a unanimous Court.
